body:
The first 3 modern universities established under British rule

One of the major institutional developments following Wood's Despatch was the establishment of universities in the Presidency towns of British India.

In 1857, universities were established at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. All 3 were modelled on the University of London. Their early functions were mainly to conduct examinations, affiliate colleges and award degrees.

This distinction is important: an examining university sets academic requirements, conducts or supervises examinations and awards recognised qualifications, while an affiliated college provides much of the classroom teaching.

University of the Punjab1882LahoreImportant later university in northwestern India
University of Allahabad1887AllahabadAnother important university of the colonial period

The establishment of universities created pathways into law, administration, teaching and other professions. However, higher education remained accessible to a relatively small section of society during much of the colonial period.

The Hunter Education Commission, 1882

In 1882, Viceroy Lord Ripon appointed the Indian Education Commission, chaired by Sir William Wilson Hunter.

The commission reviewed educational development, particularly elementary and secondary education. It emphasised the expansion of primary education, the importance of local administration in its management and a greater role for non-government institutions in secondary education.

The Hunter Commission did not establish the 1857 universities. It examined educational progress after the earlier policies had been introduced.

The Indian Universities Commission and Act

In 1902, during the viceroyalty of Lord Curzon, the government appointed the Indian Universities Commission to examine conditions in higher education.

Its recommendations contributed to the Indian Universities Act of 1904. The Act sought to reform university administration and improve standards, while also strengthening official influence over universities and affiliated institutions.

This created a tension between the stated aim of improving educational quality and Indian demands for greater institutional independence.

How to distinguish the measures

  • 1854: Wood's Despatch proposed an organised system of education.
  • 1857: Universities were established in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.
  • 1882: The Hunter Commission reviewed educational development, with particular attention to schools.
  • 1902: The Indian Universities Commission examined higher education.
  • 1904: The Indian Universities Act introduced changes in university governance and official control.

Prelims focus

  • The universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were established in 1857.
  • The early universities largely followed the examining and affiliating model.
  • The Hunter Commission was appointed in 1882 under Lord Ripon.
  • The Indian Universities Commission was appointed in 1902 under Lord Curzon.
  • The Indian Universities Act was enacted in 1904.
  • Trap: The Hunter Commission of 1882 concerned education; it should not be confused with the press law repealed in the same year.

[University Grants Commission, Genesis, historical development of Indian universities, consulted 20 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Exhibition Commemorating 150 Years of Presidency Universities (1857–2007), Ministry of Tourism, release dated 8 January 2007, consulted 20 November 2026; the Court of Directors, Despatch on General Education in India, 1854, paragraphs 23–40.]

pictures.caption: Major educational milestones from Wood's Despatch to the Indian Universities Act.

title: The Universities of 1857 and Later Educational Commissions

body:
What is vernacular education?

Vernacular education means education conducted through a language used by people in their everyday life, such as Bengali, Marathi or Gujarati. In colonial educational discussions, the term was commonly used to distinguish local languages from English.

Vernacular education is different from the study of classical languages such as Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian. A school could teach in a local language without being an institution devoted to classical scholarship.

William Adam's reports in the 1830s

In the 1830s, William Adam, a Scottish missionary, examined indigenous education in parts of Bengal and Bihar at the request of the East India Company.

His reports described a large network of local schools, commonly called pathshalas. The estimates reported in the NCERT account were more than 1 lakh pathshalas and more than 20 lakh pupils in Bengal and Bihar.

These were historical estimates associated with Adam's investigation, not figures from a modern school census. They refer to the areas covered by the reports and must not be described as totals for the whole of India.

How traditional pathshalas functioned

Many pathshalas were small institutions supported by teachers, local communities or wealthy patrons. Their arrangements varied, but Adam observed considerable flexibility in teaching.

  • Location: Classes might be held in a teacher's home, a shop, a temple area or under a tree.
  • Teaching: Oral instruction and individual attention were common. Pupils with different levels of learning could study together.
  • Fees: Payments were not always fixed and could vary according to the economic condition of families.
  • Timetable: The teacher adapted teaching to local needs. Some rural schools closed during harvest periods.
  • Organisation: Printed textbooks, regular annual examinations and formal attendance registers were not universal requirements.

The flexibility mattered particularly to agricultural families. Children who helped during harvest could return to school when agricultural work had ended.

Changes after 1854

Following Wood's Despatch, Company authorities sought to bring greater order and supervision to vernacular schools. The government introduced measures including regular inspections, prescribed textbooks, timetables and examinations.

Government-appointed educational supervisors, including pandits assigned to groups of schools, inspected teaching. Teachers were expected to maintain records and follow established routines.

Schools that accepted official conditions could receive government grants. Those that remained outside the regulated system generally did not receive the same assistance.

The effects were mixed

Regular textbooks, examination systems and inspections could create more standardised instruction and give authorities ways to assess schools. However, the new arrangements did not benefit all families equally.

For a poor agricultural household, a requirement of regular attendance throughout the year could conflict with the need for children to work during harvest. Absence that had once been accommodated by the local teacher could now be treated as indiscipline.

This example shows that uniform school rules and access to schooling are not always the same thing. A school may become more formally organised while becoming less convenient for some learners.

Prelims focus

  • William Adam investigated vernacular education in Bengal and Bihar during the 1830s.
  • His reports described an estimated more than 1 lakh pathshalas.
  • They also described an estimated more than 20 lakh pupils.
  • Traditional pathshalas often used flexible fees, oral teaching and locally adjusted schedules.
  • After 1854, official reforms promoted inspection, textbooks, timetables and examinations.
  • Trap: Vernacular education means education through a local language; it does not necessarily mean Sanskrit or Persian education.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 7, Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation, printed pp. 87–88; the Court of Directors, Despatch on General Education in India, 1854, paragraphs 41–60, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A teacher instructs children seated on mats with simple writing materials outside a thatched village pathshala in 1830s Bengal or Bihar.
pictures.caption: A traditional village pathshala where children learn from a teacher in a flexible setting.

pictures.alt: Traditional pathshalas offered local flexibility; regulation after 1854 could standardise instruction but made attendance harder for children doing agricultural work.
pictures.caption: Colonial school regulation created greater uniformity but reduced some forms of local flexibility.

title: Vernacular Schools and William Adam's Survey: Education Before and After Colonial Regulation

body:
Education created new opportunities and new inequalities

Western-style schools and universities helped form a growing class of educated Indians. Some entered law, teaching, journalism, government service and other professions. Their knowledge of English also enabled them to communicate with officials and educated people in other regions.

Education provided access to new political and social ideas. Educated Indians could read about representative institutions, individual rights and different approaches to social reform. Some used these ideas to support British administration; others used them to question the legitimacy of colonial rule.

However, access was unequal. Higher education was concentrated largely in towns and cities, and fees, social restrictions, language and limited school availability excluded many people. Women, poorer households and historically disadvantaged communities often faced additional barriers.

Education and social reform

Reformers argued that education could help challenge social practices that restricted women's lives and opportunities. Schools for girls were established by Indian reformers and missionary organisations during the 19th century.

Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar supported women's education and helped establish schools for girls. Jyotirao Phule and other reformers worked to extend educational opportunities to groups that had faced social exclusion.

Education and print reinforced each other. New readers created an audience for books and newspapers, while printed arguments encouraged discussions about education, caste and women's rights.

These developments met resistance. Conservative groups sometimes opposed the schooling of girls or feared that new ideas would weaken established social arrangements.

Indian criticism of colonial education

Mahatma Gandhi

Mahatma Gandhi argued that colonial English education could encourage Indians to regard Western civilisation as superior and become distant from their own languages and surroundings.

He favoured education through Indian languages and stressed practical work, handicrafts and the development of the whole person. For Gandhi, literacy alone was not the same as education; learning should also develop understanding, character and useful abilities.

Rabindranath Tagore

Rabindranath Tagore established his school at Santiniketan in 1901. He believed that children should learn in a natural environment that encouraged curiosity, imagination and creativity.

Tagore valued Indian cultural traditions but also favoured learning from modern science and other useful elements of Western civilisation. His approach differed from rigid classroom discipline and excessive dependence on textbooks.

Gujarat connection: Education in Baroda State

Gujarat's educational history cannot be understood only through policies implemented in British-administered territories. Parts of Gujarat were governed by princely states that could introduce their own educational measures.

Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III promoted educational reform in Baroda State. In 1906, his administration introduced free and compulsory primary education throughout the state. This was an important regional initiative in widening access to elementary education.

The Baroda example illustrates the difference between an educational policy issued for British India and reforms undertaken by a princely ruler. The two developed within the broader colonial period but did not have identical administrative origins.

Distinguish the Gujarat fact

Baroda State, 1906: free and compulsory primary education under Sayajirao Gaekwad III. This was a princely-state reform, not a provision that Wood's Despatch had automatically made compulsory across British India in 1854.

Education's wider political effect

Educated Indians later organised associations, wrote petitions and edited newspapers. The knowledge and communication skills acquired through colonial institutions could therefore be used to criticise colonial policies.

Education alone did not produce Indian nationalism. Political exclusion, economic grievances, racial discrimination and other experiences of colonial rule also contributed. Education supplied important means of expressing and organising these concerns.

Prelims focus

  • Colonial universities helped develop an English-educated professional class.
  • Education supported social reform, but access remained unequal.
  • Gandhi emphasised Indian languages, practical work and handicrafts.
  • Tagore established Santiniketan in 1901 and favoured creative learning in a natural environment.
  • Sayajirao Gaekwad III introduced free and compulsory primary education throughout Baroda State in 1906.
  • Trap: Baroda's education reform was a princely-state initiative, not a nationwide British law.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 7, printed pp. 89–91, and chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 94–99; Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Visionary Maharaja of Baroda, section on free and compulsory primary education, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Gandhi emphasised languages, work and whole-person development; Tagore emphasised nature, creativity and openness. Both sought alternatives to colonial schooling.
pictures.caption: Gandhi and Tagore offered different alternatives to conventional colonial schooling.

title: Social Effects of Colonial Education: Reform, Inequality and the Gujarat Experience
